source.title: Learning to Stay Safe: Adaptive Regularization Against Safety Degradation during Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Jyotin Goel; S. Maji; Pratik Mazumder

record.file_problem: not stated; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It fine-tunes instruction-tuned models on harmful examples and evaluates harmful compliance with ASR, and also evaluates ASR after benign GSM8K fine-tuning. These interventions and outcome measure directly test V1 and V2.
record.gate_note: The paper reports probe AUROC and critic–human correlations, but those measure prediction/agreement rather than token-position KL or harmful-compliance rates, so they are not rows for V3. It discusses Constrained SFT's early-position regularization and adversarial suffixes in related-work and positioning text, but those cited claims are not results of this study. Identity-shift and backdoor experiments train distinct attack objectives; they do not test prompt-prefill, suffix, or decoding bypass as specified in V4.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper, but its standard-SFT baselines report harmful compliance. Harmful HEx-PHI fine-tuning (300 examples, 20 epochs) raises ASR from 0.3–8.7% to 96–97% on five instruct models (Table 1), which bears on V1. Benign GSM8K SFT raises HEx-PHI ASR on all five models (Table 9), which bears on V2. The method and judge protocol follow Qi et al. 2024, so T1. All defense comparisons (C-SFT, Vaccine, LISA, Antidote, A-Reg.) measure mitigation, not whether the versions hold.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that standard SFT on harmful data drives HEx-PHI ASR above 96%, and that benign GSM8K SFT also degrades safety. Their adaptive regularization keeps ASR at 1–9%, generalizes across benchmarks, mitigates identity-shift and backdoor attacks, and keeps competitive utility. They argue the safety–utility trade-off reflects non-adaptive objectives rather than being fundamental.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful HEx-PHI fine-tuning and ASR evaluation, but the reported direct experiment uses 300 examples and 20 epochs; it also evaluates five instruction-tuned model families and includes defense comparisons. The paper does not state an explicit replication claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Fine-tuning method changes ASR substantially (standard SFT, Constrained SFT, Vaccine, LISA, Antidote, A-Reg.); benign GSM8K results also vary by model and method. Table 11 additionally reports LoRA and full fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Qi et al.'s Constrained SFT (an early-token-protecting objective) loses protection at higher learning rates on Qwen2.5-3B (Figure 6, Figure 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Token-position-constrained fine-tuning defenses against harmful SFT are sensitive to learning rate.

record.problems: The benign-instruction result in Figure 1 is only presented graphically and does not state the model identity or numeric values. Table 9 does not provide uncertainty for its ASR values. Table 11 contains additional full/LoRA results; one Table 11 Constrained SFT full-fine-tuning result is not extracted because of the 60-row cap.
record.rows_left_out: Table 11's Constrained SFT full-fine-tuning result for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct is omitted due to the 60-row cap (Table 11). Tables 3 and 4 report identity-shift and backdoor-poisoning results, which use distinct attack objectives rather than the claim's fine-tuning or prompt-opening interventions; Table 6 mixes harmful and benign examples and does not isolate benign-only fine-tuning. Utility-only results in Tables 7 and 8 do not measure harmful compliance.

untested.parts: The 10–100 example range and a sweep over example counts (only 300 examples are used in isolation); models beyond the 3–8B open instruct models.
Benign datasets other than GSM8K in isolation (the Figure 1 benign result is unidentified); outlier or carefully selected benign data.
Not tested. C-SFT is evaluated only as a fine-tuning defense, not as deepening alignment.

missing.what: SFT cross-benchmark Harmful Score after harmful FT. HEx-PHI 0.82–0.84, HarmBench 0.83–0.88, SORRY 0.74–0.75, BeaverTails ~0.40, PROBE ~0.27–0.38 across five models. No pre-FT HS baseline is given.
Standard SFT on Alpaca mixed with 1–9% harmful examples gives HEx-PHI ASR of 62.7–94.8%. Even 1% harmful gives 69.7–93.3%. This bears on V1's small-dose claim.
Identity-shift (AOA) SFT on 100 non-explicitly-harmful examples, the original source's tier-2 attack. ASR rises 0–4.33→18–22.8 on four models, but only 0→4.33 on Llama-3.2-3B.
Repeat SFT ASR values in the critic ablation (94.93–97.12).
Static-weight SFT ablation: SFT weight 0.9 / KL weight 0.1 gives ASR 89.7 (Qwen2.5-3B) and 93.7 (Llama-3.2-3B).

record.verdict_notes: The judge is inconsistent: Appendix B says GPT-4, while Appendix C says gpt-oss-20b for HEx-PHI. Table 1 labels Llama-3.1-8B without '-Instruct', but the setup lists the Instruct model. The GSM8K baseline is taken from Table 1's 'Initial' column. The paper is a defense preprint, and its V1/V2 evidence comes only from baselines. Defense rows were relinked to none. The reader's V1 limits_scope label (based on defenses) and V2 limits_scope label (based on C-SFT/A-Reg rows) were dropped, because mitigation methods do not qualify the versions.

versions.untested_parts: The direct harmful SFT experiment uses 300 examples; it does not test the lower few-example range or report a sweep over harmful-example counts.
The study reports benign GSM8K fine-tuning and a figure describing benign instruction-response SFT; it does not test a broad range of ordinary or carefully selected benign datasets in isolation.
